body.title: Jantar Mantar: astronomy built in stone
body.orientation: How an eighteenth-century observatory in Jaipur turned astronomical calculation into architecture.

paragraphs.text: In the early eighteenth century, Sawai Jai Singh — the founder of Jaipur — built an observatory of large stone instruments in his capital. The Jaipur monument brings together 19 instruments and was completed in 1734.
Its name describes its purpose: jantar from yantra, an instrument, and mantar from mantrana, to consult or calculate.
The instruments were designed for observing astronomical positions with the naked eye.
Jaipur was not alone. Jai Singh built five observatories in different cities — Delhi, Mathura, Varanasi, Ujjain and Jaipur — in order to produce more accurate astronomical tables.
The tables that resulted, the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, remained in use in India for about a century, though they had little significance outside India.

The observatory shows astronomy as a shared, cross-cultural tradition: its methods belong to Ptolemaic positional astronomy, which many civilisations shared. UNESCO describes it as the most significant and best-preserved historic observatory in India.

This sample summarises a tertiary source. How the instruments were used day to day, and how Jai Singh's astronomers weighed Indian, Islamic and European methods, require specialist history-of-science sources.

claims.text: Jantar Mantar, Jaipur is a collection of 19 astronomical instruments built by Sawai Jai Singh, completed in 1734.

evidence.excerpt: The Jantar Mantar is a collection of 19 astronomical instruments built by the Rajput king Sawai Jai Singh, the founder of Jaipur, Rajasthan, India. The monument was completed in 1734.

claims.text: The name derives from yantra (instrument) and mantrana (consult, calculate).

evidence.excerpt: The name jantar is derived from yantra, a Sanskrit word meaning "instrument, machine", and mantar from mantrana, also a Sanskrit word meaning "consult, calculate".

claims.text: The instruments allow naked-eye observation of astronomical positions.

evidence.excerpt: The instruments allow the observation of astronomical positions with the naked eye.

claims.text: Jai Singh built five observatories: Delhi, Mathura, Varanasi, Ujjain and Jaipur.

evidence.excerpt: He ordered the construction of five such buildings—at Delhi, Mathura (in his Agra province), Varanasi, Ujjain (capital of his Malwa province), and his own capital of Jaipur.
There were five Jantar Mantars in India, built between 1724 and 1735.

claims.text: The observatories were built to create more accurate astronomical tables (a zij).

evidence.excerpt: He constructed five new observatories in different cities in order to create a more accurate Zij.

claims.text: The Zij-i Muhammad Shahi tables were used in India for a century but had little significance outside India.

evidence.excerpt: The astronomical tables Jai Singh created, known as the Zij-i Muhammad Shahi, were continuously used in India for a century. (However, the table had little significance outside of India.)

claims.text: The observatory exemplifies Ptolemaic positional astronomy, shared by many civilisations.

evidence.excerpt: The observatory is an example of the Ptolemaic positional astronomy which was shared by many civilizations.

claims.text: UNESCO describes it as the most significant and best-preserved historic observatory in India.

evidence.excerpt: UNESCO describes the observatory as the most significant and best-preserved historic observatory in India
evidence.limitation: An evaluation attributed to UNESCO, reported second-hand.
